label: 0–3 months
title: Newborn
note: Every baby is unique. These milestones are general guides — premature babies may reach them later.

milestones.text: Lifts head briefly when on tummy

guide.try: Do tummy time for 1–2 minutes several times a day on a firm surface. Get down to her eye level — she’ll try harder to lift her head to see your face.
guide.watch: Head wobbles up even briefly; she strains toward your face during tummy time.
guide.see: Head shows no lifting at all by 3 months, or neck feels unusually floppy.

guide.try: Lay her on her back and gently cycle her limbs in slow, smooth motions. Bath time is ideal — warm water makes movement easier.
guide.watch: Both sides move with similar frequency and strength during awake time.
guide.see: One side consistently moves much less than the other, or limbs seem very stiff or very floppy.

guide.try: Keep mittens off during awake time so she can discover her hands. Gently guide her hands toward her face so she experiences the sensation.
guide.watch: Hands drift toward her mouth or face during relaxed, alert moments.
guide.see: No hand-to-face movement by 3 months alongside other motor concerns.

guide.try: Respond consistently and promptly to every cry in these early months. Reliable responses build trust and, over time, actually reduce overall crying.
guide.watch: Different cry patterns begin to emerge for hunger, discomfort, and tiredness.
guide.see: Baby rarely cries even when hungry or uncomfortable, or the cry is consistently very weak or high-pitched.

guide.try: When she makes a sound, pause and mimic it back — this serve-and-return teaches her communication is two-way. Talk and sing constantly.
guide.watch: Soft vowel-like sounds (ooh, aah) appear during calm, alert periods.
guide.see: No vocalisation other than crying by 3 months.

guide.try: Test gently with a hand clap or rattle outside her line of sight when she is calm and awake. A clear startle confirms her hearing is active.
guide.watch: Eyes widen, arms briefly extend, or she startles visibly at sudden sounds.
guide.see: No startle response to loud sounds by 1 month warrants a hearing check.

guide.try: Hold your face 20–30 cm away — that is the clearest focal distance for a newborn. Make slow, exaggerated expressions and give her time to lock on.
guide.watch: Eyes fix on your face and stay there; she may go still as she concentrates.
guide.see: No interest in faces by 6 weeks, especially combined with no eye contact.

guide.try: Smile broadly and slowly at her during calm awake time. The social smile typically emerges at 6–8 weeks. Increase face-to-face time if it hasn’t appeared.
guide.watch: A genuine smile — corners of mouth lift, cheeks engage — in response to your face or voice.
guide.see: No social smile by 3 months.

milestones.text: Calms when held or spoken to

guide.try: Try skin-to-skin holding, a familiar soft song, or placing her against your left chest so she hears your heartbeat. Consistency matters more than technique.
guide.watch: Crying reduces or stops when you pick her up, make eye contact, or speak calmly.
guide.see: Baby is consistently impossible to soothe — worth discussing to rule out reflux or other causes.

guide.try: Hold a high-contrast card or your face 25 cm away and move it slowly left to right. Give her time to lock on before moving.
guide.watch: Eyes track across the midline smoothly from one side to the other by 2–3 months.
guide.see: No visual tracking at all by 2 months, or significant eye crossing after 3 months.

guide.try: Speak to her from outside her line of sight and watch for her to turn her head or still in response. Use her name often in a warm tone.
guide.watch: She quiets, turns toward you, or shows alerting behaviour when she hears your voice.
guide.see: No response to voices or sounds by 3 months.

guide.try: Place black-and-white cards with stripes, checkers, or a bull’s-eye in her line of sight during alert periods. Swap them weekly to maintain novelty.
guide.watch: She gazes at the pattern and slows her movement to concentrate on it.
guide.see: No visual interest in anything in her environment by 2 months.

label: 4–6 months
title: Early explorer
note: Tummy time is crucial now — aim for 30 min spread through the day to build neck and core strength.

guide.try: Continue tummy time daily and add supported sitting on your lap so she practises balancing her head against gravity.
guide.watch: Head stays upright without bobbing during supported sitting; lifts fully during tummy time.
guide.see: Head still very floppy with no control by 4 months.

guide.try: Place a favourite toy just out of reach during tummy time to give her a reason to shift her weight. Never leave her unattended on an elevated surface now.
guide.watch: She shifts her weight to one side and rotates — tummy to back usually comes first.
guide.see: No rolling in either direction by 6 months.

guide.try: Hold toys within easy reach and slightly off to one side. Dangle objects during tummy time — reaching while prone builds more muscle groups.
guide.watch: Intentional reach toward objects with the hand closing around them.
guide.see: No reaching or batting at objects by 5 months.

guide.try: Offer safe teething toys and varied textures. Mouthing is important developmental exploration — her mouth is her most sensitive sensory tool at this age.
guide.watch: Grasped objects reliably make their way to the mouth with clear intention.
guide.see: Not typically a red flag alone, but flag if combined with very weak grasp or no hand use.

guide.try: Imitate her sounds back to her then add one new consonant sound. The more varied language input she hears, the richer her output will become.
guide.watch: Consonant-vowel combinations (ba, da, ma, ga) appear alongside cooing.
guide.see: No babbling or consonant sounds by 6 months.

guide.try: Use her name consistently and pause after saying it to allow response time. Start with visual contact — let her see your face while you call her name.
guide.watch: She turns her head or looks toward you specifically when her name is called.
guide.see: No response to her own name by 6 months warrants a hearing check.

guide.try: Gentle tummy raspberries, peek-a-boo, and funny slow facial expressions are classic triggers. Find what she responds to most and repeat it often.
guide.watch: Belly laugh or sustained giggling during playful interaction with familiar people.
guide.see: No laughter or joyful vocalisations by 6 months.

guide.try: Ensure several consistent caregivers interact with her regularly. Vary your expressions deliberately — she is reading happy, surprised, and worried faces.
guide.watch: Clear preference for familiar faces; beginning to react differently to strangers.
guide.see: No differentiation between familiar and unfamiliar faces by 5 months.

guide.try: Keep face-to-face sessions to 5–10 focused minutes. Songs with actions and simple back-and-forth exchanges are ideal at this age.
guide.watch: She smiles, vocalises, and reaches toward you during play.
guide.see: Consistently unresponsive to social play — worth mentioning at your check-up.

guide.try: Build anticipation by pausing mid-game and making a ‘what’s next?’ face before continuing. This teaches her that interaction is reciprocal.
guide.watch: Fussing, reaching, or vocalising when an engaging activity or interaction stops.
guide.see: No emotional response to changes in social interaction by 6 months.

guide.try: Hold a baby-safe mirror at face level and narrate: ‘Who’s that? That’s you!’ Move it slightly and watch her track the reflection.
guide.watch: She reaches for the reflection, smiles at it, or vocalises in response.
guide.see: No visual interest in reflections or faces in a mirror by 5 months.

milestones.text: Explores objects with hands and mouth

guide.try: Offer varied textures — silicone, wood, cloth, rubber. Supervised mouthing is safe and important; remove only genuinely hazardous items.
guide.watch: She grasps objects, turns them over, and brings them to her mouth with clear intent.
guide.see: Not exploring objects with hands at all by 5 months.

guide.try: Drop a toy while she is watching and say ‘Where did it go?’ Pause a few seconds before retrieving — you are building early object permanence.
guide.watch: Her gaze shifts downward to where the object fell, even briefly.
guide.see: Not a major concern at this stage; object permanence solidifies more at 7–9 months.

label: 7–9 months
title: On the move
note: Separation anxiety often starts here — completely normal! Peek-a-boo games help babies learn you always return.

guide.try: Practise sitting on the floor with cushions around her. Sit facing her and hold out toys — reaching for them builds the balance muscles needed.
guide.watch: Sits steadily for several seconds without hands on the floor for support.
guide.see: Cannot sit even briefly with hands for support by 9 months.

guide.try: Place enticing toys just beyond reach during tummy time. Some babies bottom-shuffle or roll instead of crawling — all are valid ways of getting mobile.
guide.watch: Any method of moving forward on her own — crawl, creep, shuffle, or roll.
guide.see: No independent mobility of any kind by 12 months.

guide.try: Scatter small safe objects (cereal puffs, soft diced fruit) on the high-chair tray and let her pick them up. This is perfect fine motor practice.
guide.watch: She picks up small objects using thumb and index finger rather than the whole palm.
guide.see: Only using a whole-palm rake grasp with no pincer development by 12 months.

guide.try: Place her hands on the edge of a low, stable table or sofa and encourage her to pull up. Stay close — falls are part of learning but shouldn’t be hard ones.
guide.watch: She uses furniture or your hands to pull herself up to standing.
guide.see: No attempt to bear weight on legs by 9 months.

guide.try: Play imitation games: clap, bang, wave — then wait and watch. The game of ‘your turn, my turn’ directly builds her imitation ability.
guide.watch: She copies simple sounds and gestures you make, even with a short delay.
guide.see: No imitation of sounds or gestures by 9 months.

guide.try: Use ‘no’ sparingly and consistently, with a firm tone and clear body language. Reserve it for genuinely important moments so it carries meaning.
guide.watch: She pauses, looks at you, or changes her behaviour when you say ‘no’ firmly.
guide.see: Not a standalone concern; flag if combined with limited understanding of words or gestures.

guide.try: Wave consistently whenever someone leaves. Pair it with ‘bye-bye’ every time and make it a cheerful, dramatic gesture she will want to copy.
guide.watch: She begins waving her hand (even approximately) at departure or when she hears ‘bye-bye’.
guide.see: No waving or pointing gestures by 12 months.

guide.try: Point to yourself and say ‘mama’ or ‘dada’ often. Label everything around her — more words heard means faster language development.
guide.watch: She produces these sounds frequently in babble — they don’t need to be directed at you yet.
guide.see: No babbling with varied consonants (ma, da, ba, ga) by 9 months.

guide.try: Never force contact with new people. Hold her in your arms while engaging warmly with the stranger yourself — she takes her cue from your calm.
guide.watch: Clinging, fussing, or crying with unfamiliar adults is completely normal and healthy at this age.
guide.see: No stranger anxiety at all — complete indifference to unfamiliar people — is worth noting.

guide.try: Ensure she has consistent primary caregivers. Brief separations with a reliable person practise the healthy attachment she is building.
guide.watch: Clear preference for familiar carers; settles more quickly with them.
guide.see: No preference for any caregiver at all by 9 months.

guide.try: Play peek-a-boo many times a day — behind your hands, a cloth, a doorframe. This game directly teaches that things exist even when hidden.
guide.watch: She anticipates the reveal with smiles or excited vocalisations before you reappear.
guide.see: No enjoyment of or engagement with simple interactive games by 9 months.

guide.try: Show her a toy then hide it under a cloth while she watches. Lift the cloth with a ‘found it!’ and repeat — you are directly building object permanence.
guide.watch: She pulls the cloth away or looks in the right place for the hidden toy.
guide.see: No searching for hidden objects by 9 months.

guide.try: Give her two objects that make satisfying sounds when banged — wooden spoons, cups, blocks. Demonstrate and let her copy.
guide.watch: She purposefully brings objects together with clear cause-and-effect exploration.
guide.see: Not typically isolated; flag if hand use is very limited overall.

guide.try: Point at objects yourself constantly, naming them: ‘Look — dog!’ She is learning to use pointing as communication.
guide.watch: She extends her index finger toward things she wants or finds interesting.
guide.see: No pointing or reaching toward objects of interest by 12 months.

label: 10–12 months
title: Almost toddler
note: First words vary hugely. 1–3 clear words by 12 months is typical — point and name things constantly to boost vocabulary.

guide.try: Practise letting go of support for a second or two while you stay close. Praise every attempt even if she immediately sits back down.
guide.watch: She releases her hold and balances unsupported for at least 1–2 seconds.
guide.see: Cannot bear weight on legs at all by 12 months.

guide.try: Arrange stable furniture so she has a safe route to cruise along. Place tempting toys at the far end to give her a goal.
guide.watch: She moves sideways along furniture with growing confidence and fewer stumbles.
guide.see: No attempt to move along furniture or bear weight by 12 months.

guide.try: Sit on the floor a step away, hold out your hands, and call her. Don’t rush — walking can arrive any time between 9 and 18 months and still be normal.
guide.watch: One, two, then a few steps independently before sitting or falling.
guide.see: Not walking independently by 18 months is the clinical threshold for evaluation.

guide.try: Offer appropriately sized soft pieces (banana, well-cooked vegetables) on the high-chair tray. Let mealtimes be messy — it is fine motor work.
guide.watch: She picks up pieces intentionally and brings them to her mouth with growing accuracy.
guide.see: Not a developmental red flag alone; flag if combined with very limited hand coordination.

guide.try: Label objects and people consistently every day. When she says an approximation of a word, enthusiastically confirm it: ‘Yes! Ball!’
guide.watch: At least one word used consistently to mean the same thing — doesn’t need perfect pronunciation.
guide.see: No words with consistent meaning by 16 months warrants a speech check.

guide.try: Give simple commands with gesture: ‘Give me the cup’ while holding out your hand. Pair words with clear actions every time at first.
guide.watch: She follows the instruction without you needing to physically guide her.
guide.see: No response to simple commands (with or without gesture) by 12 months.

guide.try: Respond meaningfully to every gesture she makes — if she points, name the object and respond. This teaches her gestures have power.
guide.watch: Pointing, reaching, waving, and head-shaking used with clear communicative intent.
guide.see: No communicative gestures at all by 12 months.

guide.try: Demonstrate simple actions: stir a bowl, talk on a toy phone, drive a toy car. Then hand it to her and wait — imitation is how she learns.
guide.watch: She copies actions she has seen adults do, even with a delay of hours.
guide.see: No imitative play at all by 12 months.

guide.try: Model affection openly — hug, kiss, cuddle her freely. She learns emotional expression by seeing it, not just receiving it.
guide.watch: Leans in for hugs, pats faces, shows physical affection spontaneously.
guide.see: Consistently avoids physical affection with familiar people by 12 months.

guide.try: Stay consistent and calm — if you react dramatically, she will repeat the behaviour for the reaction. A neutral response is often most effective.
guide.watch: She looks at your face before, during, or after doing something she knows is off-limits.
guide.see: This is completely healthy developmental behaviour — not a concern.

guide.try: Play hide-and-seek with toys under cups or cloths. Progress from transparent to opaque to make it gradually harder.
guide.watch: She looks in the right location for a hidden toy, even when moved to a new spot.
guide.see: No search for hidden objects by 12 months.

guide.try: Offer toys with clear cause-and-effect: drop things into containers, bang drums, press buttons that light up. Let her repeat to her heart’s content.
guide.watch: She deliberately repeats actions that produce interesting results.
guide.see: No intentional cause-and-effect play by 12 months.

guide.try: Give her a container and small blocks and demonstrate dropping them in. Say ‘in!’ each time, then let her try independently.
guide.watch: She drops objects into containers with clear intent, and may tip them out to repeat.
guide.see: No object manipulation or container play by 12 months.

label: 1–2 years
title: Toddler
note: Tantrums peak around 18–24 months — emotions are big but language is still catching up. Consistent routines help enormously.

guide.try: Clear safe space for walking practice. Push toys and furniture give confidence early on. Most children walk by 15 months; 18 months is the clinical norm.
guide.watch: Several steps without support, improving balance and falling less over weeks.
guide.see: Not walking independently by 18 months.

guide.try: Allow supervised climbing on low, stable surfaces — it is important for spatial awareness and strength. A small foam step or low platform is ideal.
guide.watch: She manoeuvres herself onto a low sofa or step with some effort.
guide.see: Extremely limited gross motor activity overall by 18 months.

guide.try: Tape paper to the floor and offer large crayons — the floor position gives more stability and control than a table at this age.
guide.watch: Any intentional mark-making, even random lines — the intent is what matters.
guide.see: No interest in mark-making tools or very weak hand grip by 18 months.

guide.try: Encourage active play outdoors. Uneven terrain like grass and sand actually builds balance better than smooth indoor floors.
guide.watch: She moves faster than a walk with a flight phase — at least one foot off the ground.
guide.see: Not walking steadily by 18 months, or consistently falling in a way that doesn’t improve.

guide.try: Stand close and make it a turn-taking game — she throws, you catch, you roll back. Soft balls are best at this age.
guide.watch: She lifts her arm and releases the ball with forward intent, however inaccurately.
guide.see: Very limited arm movement or coordination by 18 months.

guide.try: Read board books daily and name every picture. Expand on what she says — if she says ‘dog’, you say ‘big brown dog!’ This expansion technique is highly effective.
guide.watch: New words appearing regularly — even approximations count if used consistently.
guide.see: Fewer than 15 words by 18 months, or any vocabulary loss, warrants urgent evaluation.

guide.try: Model two-word combinations constantly: ‘more biscuit’, ‘daddy go’, ‘big dog’. Don’t require her to repeat — just model and respond naturally.
guide.watch: Two words combined spontaneously and meaningfully by 24 months.
guide.see: No two-word combinations by 24 months.

guide.try: Ask ‘Where’s the cat?’ while reading and give her time to point before turning the page. Make it a game, not a test.
guide.watch: She points to named pictures in familiar books with increasing accuracy.
guide.see: Not understanding or responding to simple questions by 18 months.

guide.try: Give two-step instructions naturally in routines: ‘Get your shoes and bring them here.’ Give her time to process each step.
guide.watch: She completes both steps without being re-prompted mid-way.
guide.see: Not following one-step instructions by 18 months.

guide.try: Arrange playdates where children play near each other with similar toys. Don’t force sharing — parallel play is the developmentally correct stage right now.
guide.watch: She plays contentedly alongside another child, aware of them without directly interacting.
guide.see: Complete disinterest in other children by 18 months.

guide.try: Model empathy openly — comfort a crying stuffed animal, talk about feelings: ‘Teddy is sad. Let’s give him a hug.’ She learns by watching.
guide.watch: She pats, hugs, or brings objects to a crying toy or doll.
guide.see: Not a major red flag alone, but combined with limited social awareness, worth noting.

guide.try: Offer controlled choices: ‘Do you want the red cup or the blue cup?’ Choice within limits satisfies the autonomy drive while keeping you in charge.
guide.watch: Strong assertions of preference and ownership — this is healthy, not defiance.
guide.see: This is healthy developmental behaviour — not a concern.

guide.try: Give her a child-safe version of whatever you are doing — a small broom, a cloth, a toy phone. This imaginative imitation is sophisticated cognitive play.
guide.watch: She copies sweeping, cooking, talking on the phone with clear intentional imitation.
guide.see: No imitative or pretend play by 18 months.

guide.try: Use everyday objects — sort socks by colour, blocks by shape. Keep it to two categories at first and narrate what you are doing.
guide.watch: She groups objects by one attribute consistently before moving to two.
guide.see: No sorting or categorising by 24 months.

guide.try: Start with single-piece inset puzzles (a circle goes in the circle hole) and progress to 3–4 pieces. Guide her hands at first without doing it for her.
guide.watch: She attempts and completes a simple shape inset puzzle with some trial and error.
guide.see: No problem-solving play with fit-together objects by 24 months.

guide.try: Set up simple scenarios: pour pretend tea, feed the doll, drive toy cars. Pretend play is one of the strongest predictors of later cognitive ability.
guide.watch: She applies pretend actions to dolls or toys that she has seen applied to herself.
guide.see: No pretend or symbolic play by 24 months warrants evaluation.

guide.try: Point and name everything in picture books every day. Ask ‘what’s that?’ and give her a second before supplying the answer.
guide.watch: She names 10+ familiar objects in books without prompting by 24 months.
guide.see: Fewer than 10 words by 18 months or any regression in language.

label: 2–3 years
title: Little communicator
note: Speech should be understood by strangers about 75% of the time by age 3. If not, a speech assessment is worthwhile.

guide.try: Demonstrate jumping off a low step with two feet together. Count ‘1, 2, 3 — jump!’ and make it a game. Trampolines are excellent for this.
guide.watch: Both feet leave the ground simultaneously, even if it is just a small hop.
guide.see: No jumping or running by 2.5 years.

guide.try: Roll a large ball slowly toward her feet and encourage a kick. Large, slow-moving balls are easier to connect with than small ones.
guide.watch: She swings her leg and makes intentional contact with the ball.
guide.see: No ball play or gross motor coordination by 2.5 years.

guide.try: Hold her hand and encourage alternating feet on stairs. Narrate: ‘This foot, now that foot.’ Handrails are key.
guide.watch: One foot per step going up, with decreasing need for a hand.
guide.see: Still cannot navigate stairs at all by 3 years.

guide.try: Draw a large circle slowly while she watches, narrating the action. Then guide her hand through the motion once before letting her try independently.
guide.watch: A roughly closed curved line — it doesn’t need to be a perfect circle.
guide.see: No intentional drawing or mark-making by 2.5 years.

guide.try: Give her time to attempt dressing and undressing herself even if it takes longer. Start with easy items — socks, loose shoes — before moving to fastened clothing.
guide.watch: Removing socks, shoes, or a hat independently with some effort.
guide.see: No attempt at self-dressing or undressing by 3 years.

guide.try: Expand every 2-word utterance into a 3–4 word sentence. If she says ‘more juice’, you say ‘Yes, more apple juice, please.’
guide.watch: Consistent 3+ word sentences appearing spontaneously in natural conversation.
guide.see: Fewer than 50 words or no 2-word combinations by 2 years warrants a speech evaluation.

guide.try: Answer every ‘why?’ simply and seriously — this questioning is crucial cognitive development. ‘Because the leaves need water to grow.’
guide.watch: Persistent questioning about cause and reason — this is exactly what should be happening.
guide.see: This is healthy — not a concern at all.

guide.try: Give 2-step instructions in daily routines: ‘Wash your hands and then sit down.’ Build to 3 steps as she masters 2.
guide.watch: She completes multi-step instructions in the right sequence without reminders.
guide.see: Not following 2-step instructions by 2.5 years.

guide.try: Model correct pronoun use even when she gets it wrong — resist correcting directly. Say the correct version naturally in your reply.
guide.watch: Pronouns appearing in speech, even if mixed up at first (this is common and normal).
guide.see: No pronoun use or consistent self-reference by 3 years.

guide.try: Set up simple joint activities: build a tower together, do a puzzle as a team. Narrate taking turns: ‘My turn, your turn.’
guide.watch: She plays with another child toward a shared goal, even briefly.
guide.see: No interest in other children or cooperative activity by 3 years.

guide.try: Use a physical timer or visual token to make turns concrete. Abstract turn-taking is hard at this age — make it visible and predictable.
guide.watch: She waits for her turn with adult support, without major distress.
guide.see: No capacity for turn-taking even with significant adult help by 3 years.

guide.try: Name emotions as they happen: ‘You look really frustrated right now. That is hard.’ Emotion labelling is the first step to regulation.
guide.watch: Clear expression of happiness, anger, sadness, fear, and excitement.
guide.see: Very flat affect or only one or two emotional expressions by 3 years.

guide.try: Arrange regular contact with same-age children — playgroups, park play. She may watch more than participate at first, which is fine.
guide.watch: She notices, watches, and approaches other children with curiosity.
guide.see: Complete indifference to or avoidance of other children by 3 years.

guide.try: Name colours constantly in daily life: ‘Your red shirt, the blue sky, a yellow banana.’ Don’t quiz — just narrate. Counting through routines helps too.
guide.watch: She correctly names 2–3 colours and counts 1, 2, 3 objects with one-to-one correspondence.
guide.see: No colour recognition or counting by 3 years.

guide.try: Sort laundry together (all socks here, all shirts there), group fruit by colour. Keep categories simple and make it a shared activity.
guide.watch: She groups similar objects together and matches pairs independently.
guide.see: No sorting or matching by 3 years.

guide.try: Join her pretend play and add elements — if she’s cooking, ask what’s for dinner. Rich pretend play predicts strong language and social skills.
guide.watch: She creates imaginative scenarios with dolls, animals, or everyday objects.
guide.see: No pretend or symbolic play by 3 years warrants evaluation.

guide.try: Use possessive language constantly in daily life and help her resolve conflicts using words rather than grabbing.
guide.watch: She uses and understands ownership words correctly in context.
guide.see: No understanding of possessive concepts by 3 years.

label: 3–4 years
title: Creative thinker
note: Imaginative play is a sign of healthy development — resist jumping in to ‘fix’ their stories. Let fantasy unfold.

guide.try: Make it a game — hop to the door, hop 3 times. Many children master hopping closer to 4 years, so stay patient.
guide.watch: At least 1–2 hops on each foot without putting the other foot down.
guide.see: Still unable to stand briefly on one foot by 4 years.

guide.try: Push her tricycle to get the sensation going, then let her take over. Most children need a few weeks of practice before the pedalling motion clicks.
guide.watch: She pedals smoothly and steers with reasonable control.
guide.see: Very limited leg coordination or strength by 4 years.

guide.try: Use child-safe scissors on playdough first before paper — it requires the same motion with less frustration. Hold the paper steady while she cuts.
guide.watch: She opens and closes scissors and makes snips in paper with support.
guide.see: No fine motor control with tools by 4 years.

milestones.text: Draws a person with 2 body parts

guide.try: Draw a simple person together and name the parts as you add them. Ask her to add a part: ‘What else does a person have?’
guide.watch: She draws a head with at least one other feature (eyes, legs, arms).
guide.see: No representational drawing by 4 years.

guide.try: Build dressing time into the routine — give her extra time so she can do it herself. Start with large buttons and elastic waists.
guide.watch: She puts on most items independently and asks for help only with complex fastenings.
guide.see: No attempt at independent dressing by 4 years.

guide.try: Engage in real conversations at mealtimes without screens. Ask open questions: ‘What was the best part of your day?’ rather than yes/no questions.
guide.watch: Consistent 4–6 word sentences with correct grammar most of the time.
guide.see: Sentences still mostly 2 words at 3.5 years warrants a speech assessment.

guide.try: Ask her to tell you about something that happened. Recap events together in sequence: ‘First we did… then we…’
guide.watch: She narrates a sequence of two or more events in order.
guide.see: No ability to retell a recent event by 4 years.

guide.try: Answer all questions genuinely and simply, even repetitive ones. These questions show she is building causal and temporal understanding.
guide.watch: A variety of question types — who, what, where, when, how — alongside ‘why?’
guide.see: No questioning at all by 3.5 years.

guide.try: Compare things together constantly: ‘This apple is red. Is this one the same colour or different?’ Make it a natural part of play.
guide.watch: She correctly identifies matching pairs and spots differences between objects.
guide.see: No concept of same/different by 4 years.

guide.try: Facilitate regular playdates with the same children so friendships can form. Talk about her friends by name and show genuine interest in them.
guide.watch: She mentions specific children by name and asks to see them.
guide.see: Complete disinterest in peer relationships by 4 years.

guide.try: Board games designed for this age are excellent — simple memory games, Snakes & Ladders. Rules give structure to turn-taking.
guide.watch: She waits her turn with only occasional reminders.
guide.see: Unable to take turns even with significant support by 4 years.

guide.try: Play simple rule-based games together every day. Explain rules slowly and be consistent — she is learning that rules apply to everyone, including you.
guide.watch: She follows game rules and appeals to rules when others break them.
guide.see: No understanding of rules or structured play by 4 years.

guide.try: When she does something wrong, focus on the behaviour not the person: ‘That hurt your friend. What can we do to help?’ Repair matters more than punishment.
guide.watch: She looks away, lowers her head, or spontaneously tries to make amends.
guide.see: Absence of any guilt response may be worth noting at your check-up.

guide.try: Count through daily routines — stairs, grapes, steps to the door. The sequence needs to be heard hundreds of times before it becomes reliable.
guide.watch: She counts to 10 in sequence with one-to-one correspondence to objects.
guide.see: Cannot count to 5 by 4 years.

milestones.text: Knows first and last name / age

guide.try: Ask her name and age regularly in a fun way: ‘Excuse me, what is your name?’ Practise with relatives so it becomes natural.
guide.watch: She answers with her full name and age (or holds up correct fingers) reliably.
guide.see: Cannot state her first name by 4 years.

guide.try: Use time words consistently: ‘Yesterday we went to the park. Today we are at home. Tomorrow is Sunday.’ A simple picture calendar makes this tangible.
guide.watch: She uses yesterday, today, and tomorrow approximately correctly.
guide.see: No time concept vocabulary by 4 years.

guide.try: Draw shapes together and name them. Playdough rolling into circles and snakes is great pre-drawing practice.
guide.watch: Circles, crosses, and rough squares appearing in her drawings.
guide.see: No intentional shapes in drawing by 4 years.

label: 4–5 years
title: School ready
note: School readiness is about social skills as much as academic ones. Sharing, listening, and managing frustration matter most.

guide.try: Demonstrate skipping slowly and exaggeratedly. Most children master galloping first then skipping — both require alternating rhythmic movement.
guide.watch: She gallops with a consistent lead foot, or skips with alternating feet.
guide.see: Very limited gross motor coordination by 5 years.

guide.try: Start with a large ball bounced from close range. Move further back as she improves. Two hands together first, then progress to one-handed.
guide.watch: She catches a bounced ball consistently with both hands from a metre away.
guide.see: No ball-catching ability by 5 years alongside other motor concerns.

guide.try: Write her name in dots for her to trace first. Use sandbox writing, finger paint, and chalk on pavements — gross motor versions of letter formation build the skill faster.
guide.watch: All letters of her name written in order, legibly enough to be recognisable.
guide.see: No letter formation at all by 5 years.

guide.try: Model correct grip at every meal and gently correct hold when needed. Thicker-handled cutlery is easier for small hands to grip.
guide.watch: She scoops and spears food reliably with a fork and spoon.
guide.see: Very limited utensil use by 5 years.

guide.try: Practise with larger buttons first — dress-up clothes are ideal. A button frame (two pieces of fabric) lets her practise without the awkward angle of clothing on her own body.
guide.watch: She manages large buttons and a zip pull independently.
guide.see: Very limited fine motor development overall by 5 years.

guide.try: Encourage her to order her own food, greet people, and answer simple questions from familiar adults. The more practice, the clearer her speech becomes.
guide.watch: Unfamiliar people understand her most of the time without you needing to translate.
guide.see: Strangers understand less than half of what she says by 4 years — seek a speech assessment.

guide.try: Ask about her day at a fixed time: ‘Tell me three things that happened today.’ Structure it the same way each time so she knows what to expect.
guide.watch: She narrates events in chronological order with beginning, middle, and end.
guide.see: Cannot sequence or retell events by 5 years.

milestones.text: Understands most of what adults say

guide.try: Engage in full adult conversations in her presence. Include her — explain things genuinely rather than simplifying excessively.
guide.watch: She follows conversations, responds appropriately, and asks relevant questions.
guide.see: Frequent misunderstandings or failure to follow conversation by 5 years.

guide.try: Read rhyming books daily. Play ‘does that rhyme?’ games: ‘Cat and bat — do they rhyme?’ Make it playful.
guide.watch: She identifies when two words rhyme and can generate a rhyming word with prompting.
guide.see: No phonological awareness by 5 years needs assessment before school entry.

guide.try: Facilitate regular contact with the same children. Ask her about specific friends and remember their names — your interest signals that friendships matter.
guide.watch: She mentions specific friends by name and shows excitement about seeing them.
guide.see: No peer relationships at all by 5 years.

guide.try: Play board games with progressively complex rules. Involve her in reading the rules and explain why each rule exists.
guide.watch: She follows a 3–4 step rule set and reminds others of the rules.
guide.see: Cannot follow simple game rules by 5 years.

guide.try: Model emotional vocabulary constantly: ‘I feel frustrated when the traffic is bad. What do you feel when that happens?’ Feelings charts expand the vocabulary.
guide.watch: She labels her own feelings with words rather than acting them out physically.
guide.see: No emotional vocabulary or exclusively physical emotional expression by 5 years.

guide.try: When situations arise, name the concept: ‘You feel that was unfair because she got more. Let us make it equal.’ Real situations teach this better than abstract lessons.
guide.watch: She uses ‘fair’ and ‘unfair’ appropriately and applies the concept to others.
guide.see: No understanding of fairness or equity by 5 years.

guide.try: Count everything in daily life beyond 10. The teen numbers (11–19) are linguistically irregular in English — they need more repetition than 1–10.
guide.watch: She counts to 20 in sequence with reliable one-to-one correspondence to at least 10 objects.
guide.see: Cannot count reliably to 10 by 5 years.

guide.try: Point out letters in the environment — shop signs, cereal boxes, books. Her own name is the best starting point for letter recognition.
guide.watch: She recognises most letters of the alphabet by sight and reads a few high-frequency words.
guide.see: No letter recognition by 5 years needs assessment before school.

guide.try: Use ordinal words in daily routines: ‘You are first in the bath today. Your brother is second.’ Physical race games reinforce this naturally.
guide.watch: She uses first, second, and third correctly in context.
guide.see: No sequencing or ordinal number concept by 5 years.

guide.try: Sort objects by two properties simultaneously: ‘Put the big red ones here, and the small red ones there.’ Sorting games make this concrete.
guide.watch: She can sort a group of objects by colour and size simultaneously.
guide.see: No sorting by single attribute by 5 years.

label: 5–6 years
title: Young learner
note: Children this age learn best through play. Reading together daily for 20 min has an outsized impact on literacy.

guide.try: Start with a balance bike if possible — children who master balance first learn to pedal a real bike much faster. Training wheels are a valid alternative.
guide.watch: She pedals, steers, and brakes with reasonable confidence on training wheels.
guide.see: Very limited gross motor coordination by 6 years.

guide.try: Tracing books, dot-to-dot activities, and writing through sand or rice trays all build letter formation. Correct pencil grip now saves remediation later.
guide.watch: She copies all letters in her name and basic shapes (triangle, rectangle, diamond).
guide.see: Cannot copy simple shapes or letters by 6 years — an occupational therapy assessment may help.

guide.try: Use a lacing board or large practice shoe first. The ‘bunny ears’ method is often easier for young children than the traditional loop-swoop-pull.
guide.watch: She can make the first knot and attempt a bow, even with some help.
guide.see: Not a major concern if other fine motor skills are developing — laces are genuinely hard.

guide.try: Progress from a large soft ball to a smaller ball over weeks. Catching accuracy improves dramatically with repeated practice rather than instruction.
guide.watch: She catches a tennis-sized ball thrown from 2 metres away more often than not.
guide.see: Cannot catch any ball by 6 years alongside other motor concerns.

guide.try: Ensure at least 60 minutes of active play every day. Unstructured outdoor play naturally includes running, jumping, climbing, and balancing.
guide.watch: She seeks out active play enthusiastically and keeps up physically with peers.
guide.see: Consistent avoidance of physical activity or significant physical fatigue by 6 years.

guide.try: Ask her to make up a story and you write it down exactly as she tells it. This validates her narrative voice and improves both length and complexity.
guide.watch: Stories with a character, a problem, and a resolution appearing naturally.
guide.see: Cannot construct a simple narrative by 6 years.

guide.try: Talk about tomorrow and next week regularly: ‘On Saturday we will go to the market. What do you think we will find?’ Future planning in conversation builds tense.
guide.watch: Consistent and correct use of will/going to forms in natural speech.
guide.see: Major grammatical errors (wrong tense in all sentences) persisting at 6 years.

guide.try: Read together every single day for at least 20 minutes. Point to words as you read. Decodable phonics readers are designed to build this skill step by step.
guide.watch: She reads simple CVC words (cat, dog, sit) and high-frequency sight words reliably.
guide.see: No phonics awareness or word reading by 6 years needs a literacy assessment.

guide.try: Have genuine two-way conversations at meals. Ask her opinions and respond seriously. Mealtime conversation is one of the strongest predictors of vocabulary development.
guide.watch: She initiates conversation, stays on topic, and asks and answers questions naturally.
guide.see: Very limited conversational reciprocity by 6 years.

guide.try: Talk about movies and stories: ‘Is that a real dinosaur or a pretend one? How do you know?’ This critical thinking develops gradually.
guide.watch: She correctly identifies fiction vs reality in books, TV, and play scenarios.
guide.see: Persistent confusion between reality and fantasy at 6 years may be worth discussing.

guide.try: Model empathy visibly — help others in front of her, discuss how characters in books might feel, respond empathetically to her own distress.
guide.watch: She spontaneously notices and responds to others’ emotional states.
guide.see: No empathy or emotional responsiveness to others by 6 years.

guide.try: Resist stepping in immediately during peer conflicts. Give her a chance to negotiate — then coach from the sideline if needed.
guide.watch: She uses words to propose compromises and reach agreement with peers.
guide.see: Exclusively aggressive or withdrawing responses to peer conflict by 6 years.

guide.try: Facilitate consistent contact with potential friends. Talk about what makes a good friend and model friendship in your own relationships.
guide.watch: A specific child she consistently seeks out, talks about, and enjoys spending time with.
guide.see: No peer relationships or social connections at all by 6 years.

guide.try: Daily 10-minute writing practice is more effective than occasional long sessions. Start with her name, then high-frequency words. Correct grip and posture from the start.
guide.watch: All alphabet letters formed legibly; simple words written independently.
guide.see: Cannot write her own name legibly by 6 years.

guide.try: Use objects, fingers, and everyday situations: ‘You have 4 grapes. I eat 2. How many are left?’ Concrete before abstract, always.
guide.watch: She solves simple addition and subtraction within 10 using objects or fingers reliably.
guide.see: No number sense or basic arithmetic by 6 years.

guide.try: Talk through cause and effect in daily life and in stories: ‘Why did that happen? What could she have done differently?’ Open questions build this reasoning.
guide.watch: She explains ‘because’ correctly and predicts outcomes in familiar situations.
guide.see: No causal reasoning by 6 years.

guide.try: Sort the same set of objects in different ways: ‘Can we sort these another way?’ This flexibility of thinking is a precursor to mathematical and scientific reasoning.
guide.watch: She reclassifies the same objects by different criteria when asked.
guide.see: Very rigid, single-attribute thinking by 6 years.
